title: REST In Peace: Why LLMs Can't CRUD

segments.text: Hello. So, this talk is about agent experience. We want to put ourselves in the view of the agent. How does agents experience the environment that we give to them? We
are the Martins from AWS and we work a lot with Agentic AI. So, I want to tell you about something I call the assistant test.
Imagine you are allowed to hire um a new assistant, a brilliant assistant. The first task uh a day and you give him a task and say, "Let's book a meeting
for the engineering team, the the agent experience team for a workshop next week. We need a whiteboard because we want to do architecture." If you have a competent assistant,

to solve the task I could give to like a human assistant? What do you think? Well, we did the test. We hired all of

rate in solving the task. So, we can say it's an okay-ish assistant, but sometimes it was less reliable than a summer intern. And this is what I call
the co-pilot plateau. So, we are spending a lot of money on building AI co-pilots, smart tools that can explain everything to us. But, can they really solve the problems?
Can they do something for us? And um that is important um part, the difference between a chatbot and an agent. And that's only one word. It's
action. Because if you want to have an AI that can do something for us, we need AI that can dynamically fetch all the data that are relevant for us.
It can understand the data, it can understand the context, and then it can make decisions based on that. And after it made a decision, it can
actually do something for us. And doing means sending API calls. Not one API call, but multiple API calls to different systems. In other words, AI
needs to be able to perfectly talk to all of our APIs. And this is where we hit the wall. Our APIs that we have for many years,
they were never designed for this type of consumer. Um today we want to show you why we believe this is the case. We have some proof points, also what you
can do about it, how you can build better systems, and where to start. So first, a very short recap. You're all familiar with that. Let's talk a bit
about REST and MCP. Um So if we're looking at REST, um REST, we have those those nouns, then we have HTTP verbs um for actions, um and REST
is stateless by design. And REST is brilliant. It was super successful because it perfectly mapped how developers think about data, how we put them into a database, and then how we
expose that data. Um and since it was stateless, it actually allowed horizontal scaling, which helped us to build huge applications at scale. But REST always assumes that we fully
understand the domain, and that we can handle all those granular operations very well. And we had smart developers, like people like you, who handled like all of this
complexity. So they were reading the docs, understanding everything, thinking about orchestration, workflows, managing all the errors, put together some software that could talk to all those
REST interfaces. Well, LLMs aren't this type of consumer. Now, you might think of like, Martin, we can stop the talk here. There's MCP MCP
that that should solve the problem. Does it? Well, MCP is a good standard for connecting LLMs to a system. And MCP gives us resources. Um we have tools for
actions, and then we have prompts for reusable templates. So, MCP provides us a standardized way for discovery and how we can expose capabilities. But, it doesn't solve the
nature of of the underlying interface. So, we can say MCP is like like a pipe. It standardizes how we communicate, but we still need to decide what we
communicate, what is flowing through that pipe. And if we expose a REST endpoint by MCP, it is still the same API design we have
on on our REST API. So, and that leads to our problem, why LLMs can't CRUD. So, um let's understand some of the problems. We brought six problems. There
are a few more, but we only have 30 minutes today. So, the first one is orchestration explosion. So, if we have a complex intent, um we definitely need
some orchestration. So, usually um we put like all of this orchestration in our code, in the front end or in the back end. Um we have smart developers
doing this. Um let's imagine for like this meeting task, um we have an intent like cancel all my meetings tomorrow um if they don't have
external um attendees. Sounds straightforward, yeah? Um but look at what the LLM has to do. It has to get like the user, then the calendar
event of the user, loop through all the meetings, get all the meeting details, handle the errors for each of the steps, and roll back if something fails.
That's easily 20 to 50 API calls for a normal day. Um so that that is not that easy um for an LLM um because the LLM must
generate perfect orchestration code. And it needs to do this every single time on the fly. So, we expect it to be a full software
developer whenever the problem shows up. And then solve it the same way every single time. Um it also needs to handle race conditions between all those
dependent calls. It needs to implement rollback logic if something fails on like step three, but step one and two were successful. And it needs to manage the
state um across all these calls. And if we have a single mistake, we have a cascading failure. And this leads us to error compounding.
Well, we like compounding with money because it's it's getting more. Um well, with errors, it's [laughter] bad um because let's assume we have an agent
that is able to handle this one single API call with a 99% success rate. Pretty good, yeah? But if we have 20 calls and
we have 99% per call, we're down to 82% of success for the final workflow. If our AI is only 90 95% good with that one
single step and we have 20 calls, we're down to 36%. So, this is not a successful workflow anymore. So, the more orchestration we need, the more steps we have, the easier
the system falls apart. Another topic, um inefficiency and cost. So, uh REST API by design always returns the complete resource. That's how how it's
designed. So, if we ask about a user, we get everything for the user. If we ask about um a room, we get everything from
the room. If we ask about a meeting, we get everything about that meeting. And then the LLM has to pass all of this, even if it only needs one field. Before
that, we we had regex um and said like, "Yeah, I need this field." It's the most efficient, fastest parser you can imagine. Um now
we're giving this to an LLM, which is the least effective parser, very slow, and very expensive. Look at this response. So, we have more than um
50 fields, um um about 3 kilobytes of data. We only need the email from the user. The LLM has to go through all the data
and spend tokens on this. Um and if you calculate this, let's say an average REST response is like 1 to 5 kilobyte, we have 20 calls, so we're talking about
20 to 100 kilobytes. Average price of an LLM of the tokens, it's like 1 cent to 5 cents, and a latency of 3 to 5 seconds. That is not
fast and not efficient. And if you're putting that into a workflow that runs thousands of times a day, this is adding up very, very fast.
Another part is schema rigidity. Um so, REST always requires perfect schema conformance. So, exact field names, exact types, exact formats. LLMs don't think that way. We have built
them differently. They are probabilistic. So, they're very flexible. They interpret an intent, and then they found like similar words to describe something. Look at this example. So, we're asking
for private or confidential, and the LLM might say like, "Ah, private, private, yeah, team. Team is a good thing." Uh or internal. Semantically the same, but the API will
reject all of those um requests. And if you say like, "Martin, that's not that difficult." Try try a few different things. Like, try dates for instance. Um
uh ISO formats, time zones, recurrences. It's not getting better if you try this. The fourth problem, error messages. Error messages in REST have been
designed for humans. And we got those codes like 500, 400, 200s. Um They were not designed for agents. For instance like 409, you learned something today that is
a real HTTP error code, 409 conflict. Um well, the agent knows something has conflicted. But now what? What has conflicted? Why did it conflict? How to resolve this? Should
the agent retry? Should the agent modify the request? Should the agent give up because he can't solve the problem? You don't know this from the error code.
So, traditional status codes in HTTP are for human developers. So, they get a code and they could spend hours on debugging the code. But those error codes are useless for
autonomous decision-making. So, agents need a semantic error message to have automatic decision-making. So, we need machine-actionable guidance for the agents. Another topic, very short, um
stateless versus stateful. REST APIs are stateless by design and we like this about REST APIs. AI workflows are stateful. This is a different mental
model which is per se not compatible. So, we're shifting like all the responsibility to handle the stateless interface to our agent. Have you monitored how good an agent can
keep the state over the time in the context window? Um, it's not made for that. Um, and the sixth problem is um discovering documentation. So, LLMs must understand
our API from the documentation alone. So, REST docs are written for humans. Developers read them and they also read between the lines. And if you have
worked on an API and you're really familiar with that API, you will know like, "Ah, yeah, I do this differently because of and so on." Um,
and developers can ask questions um to the team who has built the API and so on. LLMs are surprisingly good at reading. They can read much faster than
humans can. Um, they're really good at understanding natural language. They're good at understanding syntax patterns. They're good at um very good at grouping those related endpoints and so on. But,
they struggle with field semantics because they're probabilistic. They are not good with unclear descriptions, um with business rules that are not explicitly mentioned in the APIs, with
constraints, uh with minimal or wrong examples. Like put a wrong example, the API call will be different. Um or with implicit assumptions that we
have for that API that only the humans know because they have worked with that API. So, human developers were great because they could fill that gap. Like
we had bad documentations a documentation and then the human developer know like how to how to write the right code for that API because the
human developer had gathered like all the context. LLMs can't do this because that's the only context we give them. So, they take the documentation
literally. But it was never written to be fully taken literally. So, if we summarize this, we have APIs that require complex orchestration, return way too much data,
ask us for like a perfect schema conformance, provide error messages that not always helpful, um don't support stateful workloads, and sometimes they are hard to discover.
This is what we are giving to our agents and ask them to be super successful the very first time they meet that API. Well, I don't wonder why we are
struggling with our agents and this is what we are seeing in the market right now that a lot of agentic AI workloads are failing

your past. Um today we want not only want to talk about problems, we also want to talk about a solution and Martin is talking about the solution.
